chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn 'Umar, from Muhammad ibn 'Uthafir, from 'Umar ibn Yazid, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man's oath of manumission without a firm intention to do so. He said: 'Whoever swears by it, and Allah is pleased with it, it is binding upon him between himself and Allah, and it is not binding on the one who is compelled.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is to be understood as indicating recommendation (istihbab), because we have clarified that the oath of manumission is not binding (lazim), and likewise the oath without accompanying intention is not obligatory (wajib), except that if the matter is so, fulfilling it is recommended if Allah is pleased with it, according to what this report encompasses, adding to what we have previously explained.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an oath of manumission made without firm intention in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the strict legal binding nature of an oath and its spiritual merit, ruling that an oath of manumission without firm intention is recommended (mustahabb) rather than obligatory. Shaykh al-Tusi’s narrator, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, contextualizes this by noting that while the oath is not legally enforceable in the same way as a deliberate vow, fulfilling it remains virtuous if it pleases God, thereby reconciling the apparent contradiction with other rulings on oaths. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance between *lazim* (binding) and *mustahabb* (recommended) in the context of *yamin al-'itq*.
